name: Death Note
blurb: A student finds a notebook that kills anyone whose name he writes in it
title: Death Note Summary: Full Story and Ending Explained
description: Death Note summary: who Light, L, Ryuk and Misa are, the battle of wits arc by arc, the anime's ending explained and the main themes of the series.
h1: Death Note: Summary, Characters and Ending Explained
answer: Death Note is a Japanese anime series of 37 episodes made by Madhouse and directed by Tetsurō Araki, broadcast from October 2006 to June 2007. It adapts the manga written by Tsugumi Ohba and drawn by Takeshi Obata, serialized in Weekly Shōnen Jump from 2003 to 2006. Light Yagami, a brilliant high-school student, picks up a notebook dropped by a death god: anyone whose name is written in it dies. He decides to use it to rid the world of criminals, and the story becomes a battle of wits between Light and L, a reclusive detective determined to catch him.

head: Character
Who they are
rows: Light Yagami
A top student in Tokyo, son of a senior police officer
Ryuk
A bored shinigami (death god) who drops his notebook into the human world
L
A world-famous, eccentric detective who never shows his face; he also uses the alias Ryuzaki
Misa Amane
A popular young model and actress who reveres the mysterious killer
Rem
A shinigami attached to Misa, protective of her
Soichiro Yagami
Light's father, chief of the police task force hunting the killer
Near and Mello
Two young prodigies raised as possible successors to L
Teru Mikami
A prosecutor with a rigid sense of justice
Kiyomi Takada
A news presenter and former university classmate of Light
Touta Matsuda
A cheerful, clumsy young member of the task force

ol: Kira versus L (episodes 1–12). Light finds the Death Note: a person dies, of a heart attack unless another cause is written, if the writer knows their face and real name. Ryuk, its owner, follows him around, visible only to those who have touched the notebook. Light starts killing criminals around the world, and the public names the killer Kira. L tricks Kira with a televised challenge and narrows him down to the Kanto region of Japan. Light kills the FBI agents sent to Japan, including Raye Penber, while L comes to suspect him personally, enrols at the same university and makes him a member of the investigation team so he can watch him.

The second Kira (episodes 13–17). Misa Amane obtains a second notebook and trades half her remaining life for shinigami eyes, which show anyone's name and lifespan. She finds Light and pledges herself to him. L has her arrested. To escape suspicion, Light has himself locked up too, then gives up ownership of the notebooks, which wipes his and Misa's memories of them.

The Yotsuba arc (episodes 18–25). The notebook passes to Kyosuke Higuchi, an executive at the Yotsuba Group who uses it to kill business rivals. Light, now innocent and memory-free, genuinely works with L to catch him. When Higuchi is caught, Light touches the notebook, regains his memories and kills Higuchi with a hidden scrap. A false rule Light had planted makes him and Misa look innocent. When L plans to test that rule, Rem, who knows that Light means to use Misa as a pawn, writes L's name and that of his assistant Watari to protect her, and turns to dust, since a shinigami who saves a human that way dies.

Near and Mello (episodes 26–37). Years later Light leads the task force as the new L while secretly continuing as Kira, now with followers worldwide. Near works with the US government, and Mello, working with the mafia, kidnaps Light's sister to get the notebook. Light's father dies after a raid on Mello's hideout. Light chooses Mikami, a fanatical supporter, to act as Kira, and Takada as Kira's spokesperson. Mello kidnaps Takada; she kills him with a hidden page, and Light then has her die by writing that she burns herself. Near arranges a meeting with Light and the task force at the Yellow Box warehouse.

body: At the warehouse Light expects Mikami, hidden outside, to write down everyone's names except his own. Nobody dies: Near's team had found Mikami's notebook and swapped it for a fake, so the names had no effect. The page Mikami wrote lists everyone in the room except Light, which proves who Kira is. He laughs and confesses, saying he is the god of a new world. When he tries to write Near's name on a scrap hidden in his watch, Matsuda shoots him. In the anime, Light escapes the warehouse in the confusion and staggers away, badly wounded. Ryuk, who had told him at the start that he would write Light's name when the time came, decides the game is over and writes it. Light dies alone on a flight of steps, seeing a vision of L as his life fades. In the manga he dies inside the warehouse, in front of Near and the task force.

Ryuk was never on Light's side: he only wanted to be entertained, so the death god finishing the story is the end the rules always promised. Near's victory also completes L's work, since he builds on what L uncovered.

The meaning is debated. Many viewers read Light as a cautionary figure: a gifted young man who starts out wanting justice and becomes a mass murderer who believes he is a god. Others take the story as an open question about whether Kira's world, in which crime fell, was worse than the one before. Ohba has said he did not write the series with a particular message in mind; when asked, he offered only that people all die one day and should make the most of their lives.

ul: Justice and power: Light's wish to punish criminals turns into a license to kill anyone who stands in his way.
Absolute power corrupts: the notebook makes Light a judge with no checks, and he begins to see himself as a god.
Two kinds of genius: Light and L mirror each other, and both bend rules and use people to win.
Death: shinigami treat human lives as entertainment and lifespan as something to bargain with, as Misa does with her eyes.
Public opinion: crowds, the media and governments come to support Kira, showing how fear and order can win people over.
Length: 37 episodes of about 23 minutes; original language Japanese.
Original: the manga by Tsugumi Ohba and Takeshi Obata, 108 chapters in 12 volumes (2003–2006); the anime follows it closely but compresses the second half.
Other versions: Japanese live-action films (2006), a Japanese TV drama (2015) and an American film (2017), each changing the story.
Content advisory: frequent deaths, murder, violence and some suicide; it is aimed at teenagers and adults.

check.q: What does Light need to kill someone with the Death Note?
options: A photograph and a lock of hair
check.why: The notebook works only if the writer knows the person's face and real name.
Rem writes L's name to protect Misa, and dies as a result.

check.q: Who writes Light's name in the end?
check.why: Ryuk writes Light's name once Light has lost, as he had said he would.

faq.a: A deal a shinigami can offer a notebook owner: in exchange for half their remaining life, the human can see anyone's real name and lifespan above their head. Misa and later Mikami make the deal; Light refuses it.

faq.q: Is the Death Note anime ending different from the manga?
faq.a: The events are the same, but the anime has Light flee the warehouse and die alone on a staircase seeing L, while in the manga he dies in the warehouse in front of everyone.

faq.q: Why did Ryuk drop the Death Note?
faq.a: He was bored in the shinigami realm and wanted to see what a human would do with it. He makes clear that he is neither Light's friend nor his enemy.
